adults.title: The Lord Has the Right Person
adults.big_idea: We are good enough to teach the gospel of Jesus Christ, not because of what we know, but because we can love the Master Teacher, and He promises to help us.
adults.objective: Learners will name the promise the Savior attaches to His invitation to teach and choose one person they teach whom they will love more deliberately this week.
prepare: Read Brother Reid's talk, marking paragraphs T35.04–11 (the pattern of invitation and promise) and T35.31–36 (the shorter lesson).
Write on the board: The Lord invites ___. The Lord promises ___.
Bring paper and pencils for everyone.
Pray by name for the people who will be in the room.

segments.name: The quiet question
steps: After the prayer, tell the class that Brother Reid, newly sustained in the Sunday School General Presidency, said he felt inadequate, overwhelmed and out of place. Read the first key quote aloud.
Give everyone paper. Allow one silent minute to finish this sentence in writing: I have wondered whether I was the right person when…
Invite two or three to share only what they are comfortable sharing. Thank each one; do not correct or solve.
Point out that Brother Reid says the Lord invites all of us to teach: in classrooms, in the mission field, at home, and one by one. Everyone in this room is a teacher of someone.
questions: Where do you teach the gospel right now, whether or not you hold a teaching calling?

segments.name: Find the pattern: invitation and promise
steps: Explain that Brother Reid noticed a pattern in how the Savior calls teachers. Do not say what it is yet.
Form three groups. Assign Matthew 4:19, Alma 17:10–11, and Exodus 4:10–12. Each group fills in the two blanks on the board for its passage. Allow three minutes.
Have each group report in one sentence. Write their answers under the two headings.
Read the second key quote together. Note what Brother Reid said of the fishermen: the Savior did not expect them to become master teachers before they followed Him.
questions: What does it change for you to know the promise comes with the invitation, and not after you have proved yourself?
When has the Lord made more of your teaching than you brought to it?

segments.name: The love of the messenger
steps: Retell briefly: Brother Reid's first classroom was his home in the village of Leone, American Samoa, with 13 children and two faithful parents under one roof. His father joined the Church as a young man; his mother had limited formal education. What they had was deep faith in Jesus Christ. Many of his earliest Primary classes met in the shade of a mango tree, and what he remembers most about his teachers is how they loved the children and knew them by name.
Pair-share for three minutes: Think of someone who taught you the gospel. What do you remember most, the lessons or the person? What did that person do that helped you feel the Savior's love?
Read the third key quote. Then read 3 Nephi 17:5–10, 21 aloud, with learners listening for what the Savior did after He had told the people to go home and ponder.
Share Brother Reid's observation that class had ended, but the Savior's love for the people had not.
questions: What does the Savior's example in 3 Nephi 17 suggest about what happens before and after a lesson?
Brother Reid and his wife learned in the Australia Sydney Mission that the surest way to love those they taught was to deepen their love for the One they taught about. Why would that be true?

segments.name: A better question
steps: Tell the class that Brother Reid addressed a worry some have about the shorter lessons in the new Sunday schedule: how to teach everything in 25 minutes. He offered a better question: how can I help those I teach connect to the Savior sooner?
Read President Oaks's words (aligned quote) and the fourth key quote.
Discuss the questions below as a whole class. Apply them to home as well as to church classes.

Check for understanding: ask each person to turn the paper over and write one sentence in his or her own words beginning, I am good enough to teach because… Invite two to read theirs. Listen for the Savior's help and love, not skill or knowledge.
questions: What can a teacher or parent do that stands in the way of a learner's view of the Savior? What moves us out of the way?
If the measure of a lesson is that people leave feeling closer to the Savior, what would you stop worrying about? What would you do first?

segments.name: Choose and act
steps: Read Brother Reid's two invitations aloud. Explain that he addressed them to every gospel teacher and every disciple.

Read the promise that follows the second invitation: as we come to the Master Teacher, learn of Him and love Him, He will help us love those we teach, and that love will make our teaching more like His.

Give one silent minute. Each person writes the name of one person he or she teaches (a child, a class member, a ministering sister or brother, a friend) and one thing to do this week from the act list.
Bear brief testimony that the Lord has the right person. Tell the class you will begin next week by asking: Whom did you love more deliberately, and what did you notice?

key_quotes.text: Lord, I love You, but do You really have the right person?
Wherever we teach—in classrooms, in the mission field, in our homes, or one by one—His promise remains the same: He will help us do His work.
The impact of a gospel teacher is not just the message—it is the love of the messenger.
If class members leave the lesson feeling closer to the Savior than when they came, we have taught enough.

scriptures.use: Group 1 reads it and fills in the board: what the Savior invited the fishermen to do and what He promised to make of them.
Group 2 reads it and fills in the board: what the Lord asked of the sons of Mosiah and what He promised.
Group 3 reads it and fills in the board: what worried Moses and what the Lord promised in reply.
Read aloud in the third segment; learners listen for what the Savior did for the people one by one after the teaching had ended.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Dallin H. Oaks
aligned_quotes.text: A gospel teacher will never obscure [a learner’s] view of the Master by standing in the way.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Dube
aligned_quotes.text: We do not need to perfect ourselves to come to Christ. We come to Christ to be perfected.

invitations.text: Love the Lord and love those you teach.
the invitation is the same. Come unto the Master Teacher. Learn of Him. Love Him.

takeaways: When the Lord invites me to teach, He also promises to help me.
What people remember most is the love of the one who taught them.
A lesson is enough when learners leave feeling closer to the Savior.
act: Pray each day this week, by name, for one person you teach, and ask to see that person as the Savior does.
Before your next lesson, family scripture time or ministering visit, spend ten minutes learning of the Savior for yourself before you plan what to say.
Learn or use the name of someone in your class, quorum or ward you do not yet know well, and ask one sincere question about his or her week.
Plan your next lesson around one question: how can I help them connect to the Savior sooner?
adapt: At home or with two or three people: skip the groups. Read the three passages together and fill in the two blanks aloud; spend the extra time on the pair-share question about a teacher who loved you.
Large class: keep the three groups by dividing the room into thirds where people sit, and take one reporter from each.
Short on time: do the quiet question, read Matthew 4:19 only, read the third key quote, and go straight to choose and act.

youth.title: Qualified by Love
youth.big_idea: You do not have to know everything to share the gospel of Jesus Christ; when you love the Savior, He helps you love and teach others.
youth.objective: Youth will find in the scriptures the promise the Lord gives to people who feel unqualified, and practice sharing one truth about the Savior with love in under a minute.
prepare: Read Brother Reid's talk, especially T35.01–11 and T35.37–45.
Bring slips of paper and pens, and a timer (a phone works).
Write on the board, covered or folded until segment 3: Who felt unqualified? What did the Lord promise?
Ask the youth to have scriptures or the Gospel Library app ready.

segments.name: Write your headline
steps: As soon as the prayer ends, hand out slips of paper. Say: A news site is announcing that you have been asked to teach the gospel. You have one minute to write the headline about yourself. Funny is fine.
Have a few volunteers read theirs.

Tell them that when Brother Gabriel W. Reid was sustained in the Sunday School General Presidency, a real headline said the new leaders included men involved in Church education and an NFL player. He joked that he was glad it gave no names, because he hoped people would think he was one of the scholars.
Read the first key quote. He told the whole Church that he felt inadequate, overwhelmed and completely out of place.

segments.name: The honest question
steps: Ask the youth to show with fingers, one to five, held close to the chest if they prefer: How ready do you feel to explain what you believe to a friend who asks?
Say that Brother Reid named the two questions many of us carry: Do I know enough? Am I good enough to teach the gospel of Jesus Christ?
Take two or three honest answers to the questions below. Accept them without fixing them.
questions: When do those questions show up for you: a friend's question at school, a talk, a lesson, ministering, thinking about a mission?
What do you usually do when you feel that way?

segments.name: Promise hunt
steps: Uncover the two board questions. Divide into four teams and give each one passage: Matthew 4:19; Alma 17:10–11 (with Mosiah 27:8–10 for background); Exodus 4:10–12; Moses 6:31–34.
Set a timer for three minutes. Each team finds the answers to both board questions and prepares a ten-word-or-fewer summary of the Lord's promise. Shortest accurate summary wins the round.
Teams report. Write each promise on the board.

Read the second key quote. Point out what Brother Reid noticed: the Savior often gave a promise along with the invitation to teach, and He did not wait for the fishermen to become master teachers first. He also reminded us that the sons of Mosiah had a past marked by rebellion before their hearts were changed through the Savior's redeeming power.
questions: What do these four people have in common with someone your age?
Which promise would you most want the Lord to say to you?

segments.name: What you remember
steps: Tell the story: Brother Reid grew up in the village of Leone, American Samoa, one of 13 children. Many of his earliest Primary classes were held in the shade of a mango tree. His teachers prepared every lesson, but what he remembers most is how they loved the children and knew each one by name.
Thirty seconds of silent thinking: Who is one person who helped you believe? Then pair-share: What did that person do? Was it mostly what they knew, or how they treated you?
Read the third key quote and Elder Dube's words (aligned quote).

Explain that Brother Reid says the answer to whether we are good enough is yes, and he gives the reason: not because we know everything or always feel confident, but because we can love the Master Teacher.
questions: Why does love reach people when a perfect explanation sometimes does not?

segments.name: One-minute teachers
steps: Pair up. Each person takes one quiet minute to choose one thing he or she loves or believes about Jesus Christ, with a verse or a personal experience to go with it. Phones and scriptures out.
Partner A shares for no more than one minute while you time it. No notes needed and no polish required; the only rule is to speak to the partner, not at the floor.
Partner B answers one question: What did you feel or learn? Then switch.
Check for understanding with the whole group using the question below.
questions: Brother Reid says the purpose of a lesson is for people to leave thinking about and loving the Savior, not talking about the teacher. From what you just did, what helps that happen?

segments.name: Your week
steps: Read the two invitations aloud. Explain that Brother Reid gave them to every gospel teacher and every disciple, and that he said the Lord invites all of us to teach.
Read the fourth key quote as the promise that goes with them.

On the back of the headline slip, each youth writes one item from the act list, or one of their own, and the name of one person it involves. They keep the slip in their scriptures or take a photo of it.
Tell them you will start next week by asking for one-sentence reports. Close with your testimony that the Lord knew whom He was calling when He called them.

key_quotes.text: Lord, I love You, but do You really have the right person?
We were never meant to do His work alone.
The impact of a gospel teacher is not just the message—it is the love of the messenger.
And as you deepen your love for the One you teach about, He will teach you, walk beside you, and gradually make you into the teacher He knows you can become.

scriptures.use: Team 1 in the promise hunt: who was called, and what the Savior promised to make of them.
Team 2 in the promise hunt; glance at Mosiah 27:8–10 first to see who the sons of Mosiah had been.
Team 3 in the promise hunt: what Moses said about himself and how the Lord answered.
Team 4 in the promise hunt: why Enoch felt unqualified and what the Lord promised him.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Dube
aligned_quotes.text: We do not need to perfect ourselves to come to Christ. We come to Christ to be perfected.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Chibota
aligned_quotes.text: He sees not only who we are but who we can become.

invitations.text: Love the Lord and love those you teach.
the invitation is the same. Come unto the Master Teacher. Learn of Him. Love Him.

takeaways: Feeling unqualified does not mean the Lord has the wrong person.
The Lord's invitation to teach comes with His promise to help.
I am good enough to share the gospel because I can love the Savior.
act: Spend five minutes a day in the Gospels or 3 Nephi 11–17 looking for one thing about the Savior you love, and write it in your notes app.
Learn the name of one person in your class, quorum or school you do not know, and use it every time you see them this week.
Share your one-minute truth about the Savior with someone at home or with a friend, in person or by message.
The next time someone asks a gospel question you cannot answer, say you do not know yet, share what you do believe about Jesus Christ, and offer to find out together.
adapt: At home or with two or three youth: do the promise hunt together, one passage at a time, and let everyone share in the one-minute teaching.
Large class: run the promise hunt with several teams on the same passage and compare summaries.
Short on time: do the headline, two promise-hunt passages (Matthew 4:19 and Exodus 4:10–12), the one-minute teaching, and the invitation.

children.title: Jesus Knows My Name
children.big_idea: Jesus loves me, and I can help others feel His love.
children.objective: Children will feel that the Savior knows and loves each of them, and will choose one person to show love to this week.
prepare: Bring a soft ball, a blanket, a flashlight, paper and crayons.
Bring a picture of Jesus Christ with children (from the meetinghouse library or the Gospel Library app).
Know every child's name before class; ask a parent or leader if you are unsure.
Read paragraphs T35.16–22 and T35.25–28 of Brother Reid's talk.

segments.name: Name ball
steps: Greet each child by name at the door. After the prayer, sit in a circle on the floor.
Roll the ball to a child and say that child's name with a smile. The child rolls it to someone else and says that friend's name. Keep going until every child has heard his or her name.
Ask the question below. Then say today's truth and have the children repeat it with you twice: Jesus loves me, and I can help others feel His love.
questions: How does it feel when someone knows your name and is glad to see you?

segments.name: Under the mango tree
steps: Have the children help you hold the blanket up high like the leafy top of a big tree, then lay it on the floor and sit on it together in its shade.

Tell the story in simple words: Brother Reid is a leader in the Church. When he was a boy he lived in a village called Leone, in American Samoa, in a family with 13 children. Many of his Primary classes were outside, in the shade of a mango tree.
Tell what he remembers most: his teachers loved the children. They knew each child by name. Their love helped the children feel Jesus's love.
Read the first key quote. Ask the questions below.
questions: What did Brother Reid remember most about his Primary teachers?
Who helps you feel that Jesus loves you?

segments.name: Sing
steps: Stand up on the blanket and sing I Feel My Savior's Love (or Jesus Said Love Everyone). Add simple actions: hands on heart for love, arms open wide for everyone.
After the song, whisper today's truth together, then say it in a regular voice.

segments.name: One by one
steps: Show the picture of Jesus with children. Explain that when Jesus visited the people in the Book of Mormon, He did not hurry. He invited the people to come to Him one by one, and He blessed their children one by one.
Place the picture at the front of the room. Invite the children to walk up one at a time, slowly and reverently, and look at the picture.
As each child stands there, say quietly, using the child's name: Jesus knows you, and He loves you.
When all are seated, ask the questions below. Let several children answer.
questions: Why do you think Jesus blessed the children one by one and not all at once?
How do you feel knowing Jesus knows your name?

segments.name: Pass the light
steps: Dim the lights if you can and turn on the flashlight. Say: Jesus's love is like this light. When we love others, we help His light reach them.

Shine the light gently on the floor in front of one child (never in eyes). That child names one kind thing to do for someone, such as sharing, saying hello, helping, or sitting by someone who is alone. Then the child holds the flashlight and shines it in front of the next child.
Continue until every child has had a turn. Read the second key quote and say that everyone can teach about Jesus by loving the way He does.

segments.name: Draw someone to love
steps: Give each child paper and crayons. Ask the children to draw one person they can show love to this week: a friend, a neighbor, a teacher, someone at home, or someone new.
As they draw, walk around and ask each child, by name, who is in the picture and what kind thing the child will do.
Help the children write or copy at the top: I can love like Jesus.

segments.name: Show and promise
steps: Let each child hold up the drawing and say the person's name or what he or she will do.
Tell the children that Brother Reid invited us to love the Lord and love those we teach, and promised that Jesus will help us love others.
Say today's truth together one last time. Ask the children to put the drawing where they will see it at home. Tell them you will ask next week what they did.
Share your testimony in one or two sentences that Jesus knows and loves each child, and close with prayer.

key_quotes.text: They knew us personally—even by name.
To teach like the Savior, we must love like the Savior!
Many of my earliest Primary classes were held beneath the shade of a mango tree.

scriptures.use: In the one by one segment, open the Book of Mormon to this verse and tell in your own words what Jesus did for the children; an older child may read it aloud.
With older children, read it after the flashlight activity and ask how people can tell that we follow Jesus.
Read it just before the drawing activity and ask who loved us first.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Chibota
aligned_quotes.text: Often, helping others feel seen as children of God begins with something as simple as learning their name.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Fale
aligned_quotes.text: I am a child of God and He loves me.

invitations.text: Love the Lord and love those you teach.

takeaways: Jesus knows my name and loves me.
Loving teachers and helpers help me feel Jesus's love.
I can help others feel Jesus's love by being kind.
act: Do the kind thing you drew for the person in your picture.
Learn the name of one child you do not know well and say hello using that name.
In your prayers this week, thank Heavenly Father for someone who helps you feel Jesus's love.

adapt.younger: Ages 3–7: keep each part short and moving. Roll the ball rather than toss it, repeat today's truth after every activity with hand actions, and let a helper walk with shy children to the picture. Skip the reading; tell the story in four or five sentences. For the drawing, write the words for them and let them simply color a person.
adapt.older: Ages 8–11: have one child read 3 Nephi 17:21 and another read John 13:34–35 aloud. Ask a harder question: Brother Reid says the love of the messenger matters as well as the message; what do you think that means? Let an older child lead the flashlight activity, and use President Chibota's words (aligned quote) to challenge them to learn a new name this week.
